```{r}
remove(list=ls())
library(ape)
library(phytools)
```

Turtles and tortoises (order Testudines) span an enormous range of body sizes.
The speckled padloper tortoise of southern Africa reaches only about 10 cm in
shell length, while the leatherback sea turtle can grow to well over 2 m. New
York is home to species near both ends of this range: the bog turtle, one of
the smallest turtles in North America, lives in a few scattered wetlands
across the state, and leatherbacks visit its coastal waters. Two groups stand
out as giants: the sea turtles, and the tortoises of oceanic islands such as
the Galápagos and the Seychelles. How closely does body size track the turtle
phylogeny? And did the giant island tortoises evolve their large size after
arriving on islands, or were their ancestors already large? In this lab, we
will use phylogenetic signal and ancestral state reconstruction to find out.

The dataset for this lab comes from Jaffe et al. (2011), and includes a
time-calibrated phylogeny of 226 turtle species (`turtle_tree.tre`, with branch
lengths in millions of years) and the maximum carapace (upper shell) length of
each species in centimeters (`turtle_body_size.csv`). Both files are in your
assignment folder.

Jaffe, A. L., Slater, G. J., & Alfaro, M. E. (2011). The evolution of island
gigantism and body size variation in tortoises and turtles. *Biology Letters*,
7(4), 558-561. https://doi.org/10.1098/rsbl.2010.1084

## The phylogenetic variance-covariance matrix

We'll start with a small subtree of five species from the full dataset: the
bog turtle (*Glyptemys muhlenbergii*), wood turtle (*Glyptemys insculpta*),
painted turtle (*Chrysemys picta*), snapping turtle (*Chelydra serpentina*),
and leatherback sea turtle (*Dermochelys coriacea*). All five can be found in
New York. To make calculations easier, the branch lengths of this subtree
have been rounded to the nearest million years. Run the chunk to load the
subtree, then plot it with its branch lengths labelled (`ape::edgelabels()`
with `sub_tree$edge.length` is useful here):

```{r}

```

Pagel's $\lambda$ multiplies the off-diagonal elements of $\mathbf{C}$ by
$\lambda$, leaving the diagonal elements unchanged. The function below does
the equivalent operation on the tree itself, by multiplying every branch
length by $\lambda$ and then lengthening the tip branches so that each species
keeps the same total distance from the root. Run the chunk to define the
function:

```{r}
lambda_tree <- function(tree, lambda) {
  heights <- node.depth.edgelength(tree)   # distance of each node from the root
  tips <- tree$edge[, 2] <= Ntip(tree)     # which branches lead to tips
  new_lengths <- tree$edge.length * lambda
  new_lengths[tips] <- new_lengths[tips] + (1 - lambda) * heights[tree$edge[tips, 2]]
  tree$edge.length <- new_lengths
  tree
}
```
